newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia hardens campaign against NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia hardens campaign against NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian officials, hardening their country's campaign against NATO's eastward expansion, demanded on Tuesday the right of veto on major European security issues and said Moscow should be ready to use nuclear arms if attacked.
President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary joined the verbal offensive, cautioning NATO against offering membership to the three Baltic states on Russia's northwestern border.

Another Kremlin official openly defied Javier Solana, rejecting the NATO secretary-general's call on Monday for Russia to withdraw troops it has had in the Dnestr region of Moldova, a former Soviet republic, since clashes there in 1992.
"We will act according to the situation, and not according to what Mr Solana says," Yuri Baturin, secretary of Russia's advisory Defence Council, told reporters on a visit to Moldova.
Tuesday's verbal barrage appeared part of a Russian campaign to win concessions from NATO over the Western alliance's plans to take in former communist-ruled countries from eastern Europe.
Moscow says such expansion would threaten its security, create new divisions in Europe and give Yeltsin's nationalist and communist opponents ammunition to weaken his grip on power.

The tough comments coincided with a tour Solana is making of former Soviet republics, including Moldova on Monday and Georgia on Tuesday, and preceded visits to Moscow later this month by U.S., Italian and German leaders.
NATO member states want to create the basis for a special relationship before a summit in July at which the alliance is expected to issue formal invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Russian officials have made clear they are not happy with the terms the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is offering.
Dmitry Ryurikov, Yeltsin's top foreign policy adviser, denounced NATO's refusal to grant Russia the right to a veto on some security issues as "strange, unjust and wrong".

"Refusal to give Russia this right means actually depriving it of the possibility of taking part in settling European security problems," Ryurikov said during a discussion of NATO enlargement hosted by RIA news agency.
Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, also seemed to touch on Russia's security fears over NATO growth by saying Moscow should be ready to use nuclear weapons if necessary.

"Naturally we are not talking of a preventive nuclear strike but if an aggressor starts a war against us using conventional weapons, we may respond with nuclear ones," Rybkin told the Rossiiskaya Gazeta newspaper.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky distanced the Kremlin from Rybkin's remarks. But he drew attention to Moscow's concern over NATO expansion, making clear it would be particularly alarmed if the former Soviet republics of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia joined the alliance.

"The Baltic countries' entry into NATO would be a serious barrier between them and Russia and would have an extremely negative impact on prospects for forming a long-term model for constructive cooperation in the region," Yastrzhembsky said.

The dispute over NATO enlargement threatens Russia's relations with the West, but Yastrzhembsky held out hope that Yeltsin's planned summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next month will be capped by "major agreements".
Risking a new row, Baturin appeared sconrnful of a 1994 agreement with Moldova to remove Russian troops from Dnestr within three years.
Solana said in Moldova on Monday the agreement should stand, but Baturin said: "So far, our troops are necessary here."

The withdrawal "will be synchronised to a settlement of the conflict in the region," Baturin said. Clashes between Dnestr rebels and Moldovan forces over Dnestr's demand for independence killed hundreds of people in 1992.
